subject: psychology
title: Addiction: Explanations of Addiction
welcome_lead: Dopamine, learning theory and cognitive bias — why people get hooked.
meta_desc: A-Level Psychology addiction explanations: dopamine, learning theory, cognitive bias.
final_note: Addiction is a brain disease, a learned habit and a story.

concepts.def: Compulsive use of a substance/behaviour despite harm.
Reduced effect of drug, needing higher dose.
Unpleasant symptoms when drug is removed.
Mesolimbic system from VTA to nucleus accumbens.
Stimulus paired with drug use that triggers craving.
Distorted thinking, e.g. illusion of control in gambling.

walkthroughs.body_html: The mesolimbic pathway from ventral tegmental area to nucleus accumbens releases dopamine in response to rewards. Drugs hijack this — cocaine blocks dopamine reuptake; nicotine releases dopamine via acetylcholine receptors. Chronic use down-regulates D2 receptors, requiring more drug for the same hit.

Classical conditioning: drug paraphernalia becomes a conditioned stimulus triggering craving (Siegel 1989 — heroin overdose more likely in novel context). Operant conditioning: drugs positively reinforce via reward; withdrawal negatively reinforces use. SLT: peers model drug use.

Griffiths (1994) recorded fruit-machine gamblers think aloud — regular gamblers made 14% irrational verbalisations vs 2.5% in non-regulars. Common biases: illusion of control, gambler's fallacy, near-miss effect. These maintain behaviour despite losses.
